newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOYBEANS -- Debts cut planting in Brazil state.
newsitem.headline: SOYBEANS -- Debts cut planting in Brazil state.

text.p: Planting of soybeans for the 1996/97 crop has now started in Brazil's Mato Grosso state but producer debt problems will lead to a substantial drop in both area planted and crop size in the state this year, local cooperative sources said.
"Some areas are now planted in Mato Grosso's Lucas do Rio Verde area," said Tony Fagundes, vice president of leading cooperative Cooperlucas. "By October 10 planting should be in full swing."

"In Lucas do Rio Verde planting should be at around the same level as in 1995/96, at 150,000 hectares," Fagundes said. "But in the state as a whole we can expect area planted and crop size to drop 15 percent this year, he said.
In the 1995/96 harvest, Mato Grosso state produced 4.4 million tonnes of soybeans, some 16 percent lower than in 1994/95, according to independent analyst Safras e Mercado.
Weather in the region, where the rainy season has now started, is now favoring soybean planting, Fagundes said.
Mato Grosso is traditionally the first Brazilian state to start planting and harvesting soybeans.
"We should have our first soybeans from January 20," the cooperative representative said.
According to Fagundes, 20 percent of the producers in Mato Grosso state have debts exceeding 200,000 reais, which was the limit set by the federal government for debt securitization.
"We're suffering from a lack of resources and insufficient debt renegotiation," he said. "We'll probably recover our savings levels only in around five to six years' time."

Brazilian Vegetable Oils Association Abiove said that credit and debt problems, which are particularly sensitive in Mato Grosso state, may limit the size of Brazil's coming soybean harvest to around 26 million tonnes.

Continuing producer debt problems and credit restrictions counterbalance the new incentives given producers by the recent abolition of the ICMS tax on sales of semi-finished products, according to Abiove general secretary Fabio Trigueirinho.

In any case, the 1996/97 crop is expected to be substantially bigger than 1995/96's 23.2 million tonnes, according to Abiove figures. A recent Safras e Mercado forecast sees a six percent increase in Brazil's 1996/97 planted area to 11.4 million hectares.
Most planting should take place in the month of November, the analyst said.
Safras added that Brazil's soybean imports in 1996 are expected to total 1.1 million tonnes, of which some 800,000 tonnes have already arrived from Paraguay.
The rest should be imported from Argentina, Safras said.
A leading trader said that crushers can be expected to start importing U.S. soybeans if the domestic sales price to crushers reaches $22 a 60-kilo bag.
On September 25, the national soybean price - a composite average - was put at $17.04 a bag while prices in Parana state were quoted at some $18.32 a bag.
